answer_text:
This is a rich and fascinating topic. Here is a comprehensive answer:

---

## Human Rights in the Ancient World

Yes — while the formal phrase "human rights" is a modern invention, the underlying concepts have deep ancient roots across many civilizations. Scholars widely agree that ancient peoples grappled with ideas of justice, dignity, and natural law that laid the groundwork for modern human rights thinking.

---

### The Term Itself Is Modern

The expression "human rights" is relatively new, having come into everyday parlance only since World War II, the founding of the United Nations in 1945, and the adoption by the UN General Assembly of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. It replaced the phrase "natural rights," which fell into disfavour in the 19th century in part because the concept of natural law had become controversial with the rise of legal positivism.

That said, some notions of righteousness present in ancient law and religion are sometimes retrospectively included under the term "human rights."

---

### The Earliest Known Charter: Cyrus the Great (539 BC)

The concept of "human rights" — and what many scholars believe to be the first charter of its kind — originated thousands of years prior in 539 B.C., when King Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylonia. He issued a decree espousing religious freedom and tolerance, established the freedom of formerly enslaved and exiled peoples in these conquered lands, and allowed for captives of the former Babylonian king to return to their homelands.

Known today as the **Cyrus Cylinder**, this ancient record has been recognized as the world's first charter of human rights. It is translated into all six official languages of the United Nations, and its provisions parallel the first four Articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

---

### Ancient Mesopotamia: Hammurabi's Code (~1750 BC)

From the earliest times — for example, by King Hammurabi of Babylon around 1750 BC — laws have been written (or cut in stone) that include principles of justice, fairness, and protection.

---

### Ancient Greece: Natural Law and Philosophy

The Greeks were the earliest to have a conception of Natural Law principles — that there exist universal principles which govern the cosmos and are applicable to all human beings without discrimination.

In ancient Greece, philosophers like Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle explored the idea of natural law — the notion that certain principles of justice exist independently of human-made laws. This can be seen vividly in literature: the concept of natural rights is described in the great play *Antigone* by Sophocles, in which the protagonist fights against the ruler for her right to bury her brother's dead body with full rituals and honors.

The idea of limiting the power of the sovereign — the hubris of the tyrant — was an element of Greek political thought practically from its origins, infusing the whole of Greek political history, eventually being received into Roman thought and finally forming the basis of modern legal theory.

However, scholars are careful to note that although in antiquity there was no human-rights *theory*, from the heart of Greek political philosophy a concept of natural law emerged that served as the foundation of the political and legal order.

---

### The Stoics: A Universal Brotherhood

The Stoic philosophy focused on the principles of natural law, which were universal in nature — rights which every human being possesses by virtue of being human and rational. The Stoics also saw no contradiction in loving one's homeland while at the same time positing a common humanity.

The development of the tradition of natural justice into one of natural law is usually attributed to the Stoics. The rise of natural law as a universal system coincided with the rise of large empires and kingdoms in the Greek world.

---

### Ancient Rome: Codifying Natural Rights

Roman legal scholars, especially Cicero, built on Greek philosophy by developing the concept of *jus naturale* (natural rights), suggesting that some rights belong to people simply because they are human.

The Romans applied Stoic ideas of natural law in their provinces, creating a new body of laws — divided into *jus civile* (Roman civil law for citizens) and *jus gentium* (applicable to non-citizens).

---

### Other Ancient Traditions

In India, the Vedas and Upanishads emphasized the concept of *Dharma* — duty, righteousness, and moral order — while Buddhism and Jainism stressed non-violence and compassion for all living beings. In China, Confucian philosophy promoted social harmony, respect, and moral governance.

In 1200–300 BCE, the scriptures of the ancient Israelites formed the basis of Christian and Muslim thinking. The Ten Commandments outline respect for life and for the property of others. The principle that a person is innocent until proven guilty and the tradition of granting asylum originate in Jewish law.

---

### Conclusion

Ideas about the inherent dignity of man originated thousands of years ago, in law and religion, coming with notions such as that one should not use arbitrary violence, lie, steal, or break contracts. While these ancient traditions did not use the language of "human rights" as we understand it today, they planted the intellectual and moral seeds from which the modern concept grew. It was the philosophers of antiquity who initiated the concept of "natural law," and from the time of antiquity, the concept of human rights gradually began to emerge — subsequently, the concepts of equality and freedom of person and citizen were formed.
